claims.text: The as-deposited non-equiatomic FeMnNiGeSi alloy is a chemically disordered single-phase solid solution, potentially hexagonal.
The as-deposited alloy contains significant local compositional fluctuations.
The as-deposited alloy contains significant residual lattice strain.
Spatial variations in local chemical order and lattice strain create a broad distribution of magnetic exchange interactions.
The distribution of magnetic exchange interactions drives a sharp first-order magnetostructural transition with a large magnetic entropy change.
Regions with different exchange interactions transition at slightly different temperatures.
Transitions occurring at different temperatures give rise to a large magnetic entropy change.
Chemical and structural inhomogeneities create energy barriers that pin magnetic domain walls.
Domain-wall pinning produces significant hysteresis during low-field cooling cycles.
A controlled low-temperature anneal can enhance local chemical ordering and relax lattice strain without causing major phase transformations or grain growth.
Annealing will partially homogenize exchange-interaction regions and reduce domain-pinning sites.
Annealing will reduce magnetic hysteresis, producing narrower magnetization loops and lower coercivity than in the as-deposited alloy.
Annealing will preserve a similar peak magnetic entropy change relative to the as-deposited alloy.
The as-deposited alloy has a large, sharply peaked magnetic entropy change.
The as-deposited alloy has significant hysteresis during low-field magnetic-cooling cycles.
The predicted response applies for applied fields below approximately 1–2 T and temperatures around the magnetostructural transition.
The predicted response is limited to processing conditions that retain a single-phase microstructure within the FeMnNiGeSi compositional window.
Annealing that induces phase changes or extensive grain growth may invalidate the prediction.
Failure to obtain a statistically significant hysteresis reduction while retaining at least 80% of the baseline magnetic entropy change would falsify the proposed dominant mechanism.

contradictions.description: The hypothesis attributes a sharp entropy-change peak to a broad distribution of exchange interactions and regions transitioning at different temperatures. Such a distribution ordinarily implies transition broadening, so the asserted sharp peak and distributed transition temperatures are internally in tension and are not reconciled.
